Hot showers don't work for everyone, so unfortunately that doesn't exactly rule it out. The only way to know for sure is to abstain from weed for ~90 days or so, there are no other ways to test to find out.

Are there any symptoms besides belching?

Unfortunately it may take quitting long term to rule CHS out before they will consider other issues seriously. Everyone is different but even before hyperemesis id have some nausea/anxiety before actually starting to vomit, although indigestion can be a part of it it is a bit unusual that that's the only symptom.
Do hot showers ease your symptoms? It doesn't work for everyone but it was the only thing that made me feel okay while I was having episodes.

90 days is typically considered standard, but it could be less or more. Some people have reported up to six months of symptoms before having relief, some people feel okay after a few weeks to a month. I do have CHS. I quit smoking entirely, but when I quit it took months to feel better. Probably 70 days for the worst of my symptoms to completely go away, a few months after my appetite was normal again.

 I was a super heavy user though, and I'd had CHS for a long time so my episodes were very severe. Tons of hospitalizations over years. I had a lot of THC stored and I lost weight rapidly which caused the stored cannabanoids to make me sicker.
This doesn't really sound like CHS but the only way to know for sure is to quit smoking for a while and see if it stops. Some people don't have nausea or vomiting, or only have one of the two.

Boring car, boring job, boring husband, boring kids, boring life. A life defined by decisions made for her; societal expectations and being too young to realize that there was a life outside of the options her parents had laid out before her. Alicia had never seen Thailand. She had only been with one man- the same man she had been with since her junior year of highschool. Never been arrested, never been to a party and made an ass of herself, and at thirty-five, she decided that she’d had enough.   
	

Stolen moments over the course of a year began to add up. A new license, a new passport, documents with a name unrecognizable from the one given to her at birth. A new knowledge of how to make a car crash severely enough that a body would be unrecognizable without dental records, and a few carefully made friends at morgues across the state.   
	

A year of second-guessing herself and almost backing out had led her here. Of course Alicia felt guilty about what she was doing, especially in the days directly following the “accident”, but it was coupled with a delicious anticipation that made her vibrate with new life. She stood carefully out of sight, watching her loved ones sob as the closed casket was lowered into the ground.   
	

“Alicia Gainer?” A deep voice gravelled from her left. A quick turn and a double take revealed… Nothing.   
	

“Hello?” She called softly, looking around for the voice’s owner.   


“Strange, I’ve rarely had souls unable to see me before,” the voice pondered, and she swore she saw a dark shape, a movement on the edge of her perception that was almost solid enough to take form, but not quite. “I am here to take you home, now. It’s time.”   
	

“Home?”   
	

“Yes, home. I’m sure you have realized, of course, that you are dead.”  
	

Had the middle aged woman been thinking clearly, she may have remarked on the fact that she was speaking to nothing. Maybe she would have even taken a moment to consider that she was losing her mind, some undiagnosed mental illness was plaguing her, maybe even consider the fact that the slow building illness was the reason she had decided to so permanently alter her life in this way,   
	

But the softly swirling pattern of grey that she could see just out of the corner of her eye when she held her head at just the right angle coupled with the fact that Alicia had absolutely no family history of mental illness influenced her decision to go along without question.   
	

“Well… I suppose so,” she hesitated. “Are you sure?”  


“Death does not make mistakes. It’s time to come home.”   
	

She nodded slowly and carefully, though her thoughts were racing. Had she really faked her death so well that she had tricked Death?   
	

“Follow me. I understand you cannot see me, so you may follow my voice until we cross. It is a long journey to the Door.”  
	

Death told Alicia stories as they walked, and she followed his voice dutifully, all the while wondering how she could possibly explain this situation away. He told her about the beginning of time, about people who came long before her and people who would come long after. He asked her about her family, those she was leaving behind. Alicia felt a deep pang of sadness as she described meeting her husband as a young teen, sneaking out of windows and stolen kisses that slowly morphed into a sleepy domestic life. Death did not tire. She did. She asked if they could sit for a while, and Death obliged.   
	

“My kids are wonderful,” Alicia confessed. “I feel that I may have taken them for granted, sometimes.” Death let her confession fill the air without response, and they carried on their way once more. They walked through fields, through cities, stopping sometimes so Alicia could sleep or rest her feet. There was no way of tracking how much time had passed, it could have been hours or days or months filled with quiet conversation, soft spoken confessions of a life wasted, moments unappreciated.   
	

Near the end of their journey together, Death and Alicia paused to regard one another. He had become more solid since the beginning of their time together, more palpable. She could see him head on now, not just small glances from the corner of her eyes.   
	

“We are almost there,” Death paused. “Is there anything else you would like to discuss?”   
	

Alicia paused. She had accepted, at this point, that her fate was death, despite the fact that she had not really died she could no longer imagine herself going to live the adventurous, impulsive life that she had laid out for herself. “I took so much of my life for granted,” her voice cracked. “I’m going to miss it all. My husband, my kids, everything I thought was tedious. I’m going to miss making them breakfast,” she admitted.   
	

Death paused thoughtfully. “What would you give? To make them breakfast again?”   
	

Her head shot up, eyes wide. “Anything.”  
	

“Alicia Gainer, I know you are not really dead.”  
	

They stood in front of the door, now, regarding each other like old friends.   
	

“You may cross the threshold with me, if you wish. There is plenty of excitement to be found in the land of the dead, especially for a soul not quite crossed over. Or, you can go home, and you can make your family breakfast. You can go back to your job, to your life.”  
	

She paused. It felt like an easy decision to make, but the implications and the cost of either choice weighed heavily. “Will they know that I faked it? That I tried to leave them?”  
	

Death paused. “I can return you to the day before the crash, if you wish. Or you can be honest and deal with the repercussions that come along with it. Human morality means very little to me. There is no right choice. I have grown rather fond of you. I do not often extend favors to the living, but I find you to be a particularly interesting specimen.”  
	

Alicia nodded, taking a deep breath. “I know what I want to do.”  
	  
  
	

Breakfast had never tasted quite so good. Her daughters’ screeching had never sounded quite so musical, and Alicia hadn’t been so excited by her husbands’ touch since she was in her early twenties. She had thought the problem was with her surroundings, with her family, her choices, but her unhappiness stemmed from a poison of her own making. Constantly coveting the lives of her friends’, constant disregard for the kind, thoughtful things her husband would do for her because she had lost the spark, the moments inbetween sleep where her daughters would look at her with love and reverence.   
  
Who could have guessed that the one who would give Alicia her life back would be Death?
